title: Act I, Scene V

teacherSummary.text: Lady Macbeth reads Macbeth's letter about the prophecies and fears his nature is 'too full o' the milk of human kindness.' Hearing that Duncan will stay the night, she calls on spirits to 'unsex me here' and fill her with cruelty, and asks thick night to hide her knife. Macbeth arrives; she tells him to 'look like the innocent flower, but be the serpent under't' and to leave the business to her.

context.history: Early modern ideas of gender linked women with pity and nursing and men with violence; Lady Macbeth's invocation deliberately reverses those expectations. Calling on spirits echoed what the witchcraft laws punished.

significance: Lady Macbeth's soliloquy is one of the play's great speeches: she sees ambition as requiring the suppression of feeling and of gender itself. Her flower and serpent image restates 'fair is foul' as a plan.
